summary: When Pharisees who loved money scoff at Him, Jesus tells of a rich man and a beggar named Lazarus whose places are reversed after death.
key_insight: In torment, the rich man calls the beggar by name. He had known who lay at his gate all along. Even now he treats him as an errand boy: “send Lazarus.”
story: Jesus had just taught that no one can serve both God and money. The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they derided Him. He answered, “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is highly esteemed among men is an abomination in the sight of God.”

The Law and the Prophets had pointed the way until John, He said; since then the kingdom of God has been preached, and everyone is pressing into it. Yet not one tittle of the Law would fail. And He gave them a plain word on marriage: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

Then He told a story. “There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and fared sumptuously every day.” At his gate lay a beggar named Lazarus, full of sores, longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.

The beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried. In Hades, in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus at his side. He cried out, “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.”

Abraham answered, “Son, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things; but now he is comforted and you are tormented.” Besides, a great gulf was fixed between them, and no one could cross it from either side.

Then the rich man begged Abraham to send Lazarus to his father’s house to warn his five brothers. Abraham said, “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” “No, father Abraham,” he pleaded, “but if one goes to them from the dead, they will repent.” Abraham’s answer ends the story: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rise from the dead.”

scene.label: Purple and fine linen
scene.text: Purple dye came from shellfish gathered on the coast near Tyre, and it was so costly that it marked kings and the very rich. Fine linen, much of it from Egypt, was worn next to the skin. The rich man dressed like royalty and feasted every day, not only on holidays.

scene.label: Laid at his gate
scene.text: Luke says Lazarus “was laid” there: others put him at the gate, probably because he could not walk. The dogs were street scavengers, not pets, and unclean in Jewish eyes. He was too weak to keep them away.

scene.label: Abraham’s bosom
scene.text: At a feast, guests reclined on couches, and the honored guest leaned close to the host’s chest (compare John 13:23). The beggar who longed for crumbs now has the place of honor beside Abraham, the father of Israel.

scene.label: Hades
scene.text: Hades is the Greek name for the realm of the dead, the word the Greek Old Testament used for Sheol. In Jesus’ story it holds both comfort and torment, divided by a gulf that no one can cross.

scene.label: A story with a name
scene.text: Apart from Abraham, Lazarus is the only person given a name in any of Jesus’ parables. The name is a form of Eleazar, meaning God helps. Because of the name, some believe Jesus described real people; most read a parable, since it opens like the one before it: “There was a certain rich man” (Luke 16:1).

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells this story. He sets it beside the shrewd steward, so chapter 16 holds two stories about money: one about a man who used wealth to prepare for the future, the other about a man who did not. Luke, who records Mary’s song that the rich are sent away empty (1:53) and Jesus’ woes on the rich (6:24), gives the poor man a name and leaves the rich man nameless.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks with authority about what lies beyond death, and He sees the man everyone stepped around. In His story the beggar has a name and the rich man has none.
seeing.living: The rich man knew Lazarus by name and still gave him nothing. Mercy begins by truly seeing the person at your own gate. And the warning will not come from a voice from the dead; God has already spoken in Scripture, and in the One who did rise.
seeing.ponder: Whose name do you know but whose need you have stepped past? And are you waiting for a sign when God has already spoken?

preaching.big_idea: Listen to God’s Word now, before death fixes the gulf forever.
outline: A gulf that cannot be crossed (26)
preaching.watch_for: Read the story with verse 14: the first hearers were Pharisees “who were lovers of money.” “The law and the prophets” (v. 16) and “Moses and the prophets” (vv. 29, 31) frame the passage. John tells of another Lazarus who did come back from the dead, and the chief priests then plotted to kill him too (John 12:10–11).
